name: Thousand Pillar Temple, Warangal
deity: Shiva, Vishnu, and Surya, in a three-shrined temple
tradition: Shaivism, with Vaishnava and Saura shrines
summary: Built in 1163 CE by the Kakatiyas at Hanamkonda near Warangal, the Thousand Pillar Temple is a star-shaped, three-shrined temple to Shiva, Vishnu, and the Sun, famed for its forest of intricately carved pillars and a monolithic black-stone Nandi.

sections.history: The Thousand Pillar Temple was raised in 1163 CE by the Kakatiya king Rudradeva at Hanamkonda, an early seat of the dynasty that would soon build the great fort-capital at nearby Warangal. It belongs to the first flowering of Kakatiya temple-building, a generation before Ramappa, and its inscriptions record the endowments that sustained it. Damaged in later centuries, it has been carefully conserved, and remains both a living Shiva temple and a landmark of the Kakatiya achievement in the Telangana country.
sections.architecture: The temple is a trikutalaya — a three-shrined plan, its sanctums for Shiva, Vishnu, and Surya opening off a common star-shaped hall, so that three streams of worship meet under one roof. A pillared mandapa carries the intricately carved columns that give the temple its name, and a large monolithic Nandi of polished black basalt faces the Shiva shrine. Perforated stone screens, carved doorways, and a detached rock-cut elephant complete an ensemble whose precision — the pillars turned as if on a lathe — marks the confident early Kakatiya style.
sections.legends: The temple’s lore dwells less on a single miracle than on the wonder of its making: the thousand pillars, no two quite alike, and the great Nandi cut from a single block and polished to a mirror sheen, are held up in local memory as proof of the Kakatiya masons’ genius. The trikuta plan itself carries a quiet theology, gathering Shiva, Vishnu, and the Sun as one, so that devotees of each tradition find their god beneath the same star-shaped hall.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri is the principal festival, filling the temple through the night, and Kartika Masam brings lamps and special worship to the Shiva shrine. As part of the Kakatiya heritage around Warangal, the temple shares in regional festivals and in the cultural programmes that celebrate the dynasty’s art, and daily worship continues across its three sanctums.
sections.experience: The Thousand Pillar Temple sits amid the busy town of Hanamkonda, yet within its walls the pillared hall keeps a cool, shadowed calm. Walking the forest of carved columns, each catching the light differently, and circling the mirror-black Nandi in its pavilion, a visitor feels the assurance of a young dynasty at the height of its art. The star-shaped plan reveals itself slowly as one moves around the three shrines, and the conserved stonework, sharp after eight and a half centuries, rewards a patient, close look.

visit.timings: Generally open from around 6:00 am to 8:00 pm daily, with pujas through the day; hours extend on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is appreciated, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is removed at the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed of the exterior and pillars; follow posted rules within the sanctums and during worship.
visit.gettingThere: The temple is in Hanamkonda, part of the Warangal urban area, about 145 km from Hyderabad; Warangal has a major railway junction and the nearest airport is Hyderabad.
